frase_gancho.texto: A skull with red rays that represents the Sun as it dies.

puente_narrativo.texto: From the Sun that goes out, we move on to the fire that must never go out. Step up to the stone old man who carries a brazier on his head: the Old God, whom you already met in clay.

guion_corto.texto: In front of you is an andesite disk, more than a meter tall, with traces of red paint. At the center, a human skull with its mouth open and its tongue sticking out; around it, a halo folded like paper or like rays of sunlight. It was found in 1963 south of the Pyramid of the Sun, in Teotihuacán, but according to the museum's label it was not made by the people of Teotihuacán: it was made by the Mexica, centuries later. It is related to the Sun as it sets in the west: the Earth swallows it to light the world of the dead, and then lets it be reborn in the east. An image that is cold and luminous at the same time.

guion_largo.texto:
Archaeologists found it in 1963, south of the Pyramid of the Sun, in Teotihuacán. It is made of andesite, a volcanic stone, and still bears traces of red paint. Here comes a surprise: although it was found in a Teotihuacan city and sits in this hall, the museum explains that it was not made by the people of Teotihuacán, but by the Mexica, between the years 1200 and 1521. Teotihuacán had been abandoned for centuries when they arrived, and they considered it a sacred place. Perhaps the disk was part of an offering they left there.

Notice that this is not a “sad” skull. Its mouth is open, its teeth are showing, and a tongue sticks out, as if it were speaking, or singing, or devouring. The halo around it is made of slanted grooves, and it has been compared to folded paper, to a fan of feathers, and to rays of sunlight. That is why it is related to the death of the Sun: a skull that frightens and lights up at the same time.

For the Mexica, the Sun died every day. At dusk it went down to the world of the dead, and the next morning it had to be born again. They said the Sun rose accompanied by warriors who had died in battle and set accompanied by women who had died in childbirth. That idea explains why a skull can be, at the same time, a Sun.

There is a detail that repeats: the tongue. In the Mexica Hall, the [Sun Stone](mna_s06_piedra_sol) has at its center a face whose tongue is a flint knife, a symbol of sacrifice. Since both are Mexica work, it makes sense that they share that image. When you see that face, remember this one.

No one knows for certain what this disk was for. It may have been part of an altar or an offering in front of the pyramid. That it was found there suggests a solar ritual, but that is a hypothesis. Its size, over a meter, suggests that it could be seen well from a certain distance, and the red paint made it even more striking.

The Pyramid of the Sun is one of the largest in the Americas, and beneath it runs a tunnel that ends in a cave-shaped chamber that, according to several archaeologists, may be what made the place sacred. Many Mesoamerican cultures saw in caves the entrance to the underworld and the origin of peoples. A sun that dies before a pyramid built over a cave: the image comes full circle.

That is why it is worth looking at this disk as a clock: a sun that hides and returns, again and again, while the city rises, transforms and, in its time, also goes out.

texto: Look at the skull and the tongue sticking out of its mouth
Find the traces of red paint on the stone
Notice the rays of the halo: do they look like folded paper or sunlight?

texto.Origin: Teotihuacán, State of Mexico (south of the Pyramid of the Sun)
texto.Dimensions: 1.26 m high x 1.02 m wide x 0.25 m thick
texto.Discovery: Found in 1963 south of the Pyramid of the Sun

texto.pregunta: Myth: It is a Teotihuacan disk because it was found in Teotihuacán.
texto.respuesta: Reality: It was found there, but the museum attributes it to the Mexica, who arrived at the ruins centuries after the city was abandoned.
